m: An award or expression of praise.
e: French accolade, an embrace, from Latin ad + collum (neck). The knight’s ceremony included an embrace or a tap on the neck with the sword.
t: The king dubbing a knight with an embrace around the neck (collum). Today: an honour, a prize.
Same as « admonester ». Monere = warn, like a monitor.
Thesis vs antithesis: placed against each other. « Aux antipodes ».

m: Based on random choice or personal whim, not reason.
e: Latin arbitrarius, from arbiter (judge). Left to the judge’s discretion.
t: Same as « arbitraire »: whatever the arbitre decides on a whim.

e: Latin arcanus (secret), from arca (chest, box). Locked in a box.
t: « Les arcanes du pouvoir »: secrets locked in a chest (arca).

m: Willingness to take bold risks; rude boldness.
t: « L’audace ». Can be praise (bold) or blame (the audacity to ask!).

m: Severe or strict; plain, without comfort.
e: Greek austēros (harsh, bitter, making the tongue dry), via Latin austerus.
t: Same as « austère ». A monk’s cell: bare walls, no comfort.

e: Old English bræsen (made of brass). Brass = hard and loud, hence shameless.
t: A face made of brass: no blush possible. A brazen lie.

e: Latin circumscribere: circum (around) + scribere (to write, draw). Drawing a line around.
t: Same as « circonscrire »: drawing a circle around something (une circonscription).

m: A component part; a voter in a district.
t: The parts that constitute something, or the voters who constitute a constituency.

m: A person with superficial interest in an art or subject.
e: Italian dilettante (lover of the arts), from dilettare (to delight), Latin delectare.
t: Same as « dilettante »: dabbling for delight, never mastering.

m: To stir up trouble or rebellion.
e: Latin fomentare, from fomentum (a warm poultice), from fovere (to warm).
t: Same as « fomenter un complot »: keeping a revolt warm until it hatches.
Garrire = to chatter like a bird. A garrulous seatmate on a long flight.

e: French gauche (left; clumsy), probably from Frankish welkan (to wilt).
t: Exactly French « gauche »: clumsy, like doing everything with the left hand.

e: English hap (luck, from Old Norse happ) + hazard (chance, via French hasard from Arabic az-zahr, the die).
t: Hap + hasard = luck + luck. Nothing planned.

m: Dominance of one group or state over others.
t: Same as « hégémonie »: Athens leading the other Greek cities.
In-amicus = not a friend → « ennemi ». Conditions inimical to growth.
Can’t be scrutinised. An inscrutable poker face.
Same as « insolent ».
Same as « intrépide »: no trépidation.

m: Having a long-established habit unlikely to change.
e: Latin inveteratus (grown old), from vetus (old), as in veteran.
t: Same as « un fumeur invétéré ». A veteran habit.

m: Not able to be changed or reversed.
t: Same as « irrévocable »: can’t be called back.

m: To treat someone as a celebrity.
e: From lion, in the 18th-century sense “a celebrity”: from the custom of taking visitors to see the lions at the Tower of London.
t: Treat someone like the star attraction: the lion everyone queues to see.
A maker of gifts. Same as « munificent » (rare in French).
« Une myriade d’étoiles ». Literally 10,000.

m: Excessively eager to please or obey.
t: Same as « obséquieux »: following someone everywhere to please them.

e: Greek ostrakizein, from ostrakon (pottery shard). Athenians voted to exile someone by writing his name on shards.
t: Picture Athenians scratching a name on a broken pot to banish him.

e: Latin pedester (on foot; prosaic), from pes, pedis (foot). Prose was “on foot”, poetry had wings.
t: Not the person crossing the road: a style that plods on foot instead of flying.

m: Having a harmful effect, especially gradually.
t: Same as « pernicieux ». Nex = death, slowly.

m: Evoking a keen sense of sadness.
t: Same as « poignant »: it pricks your heart (pungere, as in punctuation).
Head first over the précipice. A precipitous drop in sales.

m: Remarkably great in size or degree.
t: Same as « prodigieux »: like an omen, it amazes.
Same as « prolifique »: lots of offspring.

m: Favourable; indicating a good chance of success.
t: Propitious = « propice »: « un moment propice ».

e: Old French ravineus (violent, rapacious), from raviner (to ravage), Latin rapina (plunder).
t: Hungry enough to plunder (rapina, as in « rapine »). Not from the bird raven.
« Répudier sa femme »: in Rome, a formal divorce. Repudiate a claim = cast it off.
Scindere = scinder, to cut: rescinding a contract cuts it off.

m: Increasing or reviving after a period of decline.
t: Rising again, like resurrection. « Une résurgence ».

e: Latin reverentem, from revereri (to stand in awe of).
t: « Faire la révérence »: a deep, respectful bow.

e: Latin sanctio (decree, penalty), from sancire (to make sacred, decree).
t: A decree can approve or punish. On the GRE it often means approve: « entériner ».

e: Latin scrupulosus, from scrupulus (small sharp stone; a pang of conscience).
t: Same as « scrupuleux »: feeling every tiny pebble in your shoe.
Seeds scattered when sowing (as in spore). « Sporadique ».

m: Seeking to undermine an established system.
e: Latin subvertere: sub (under) + vertere (to turn). Turning upside down from below.
t: Same as « subversif »: turning the system over from underneath.

e: Greek sykophantēs (informer), literally “fig-shower”: sykon (fig) + phainein (to show). Origin of the image debated.
t: The fig-shower: picture a courtier offering figs to the king, nodding at every word.
Same as « taciturne ». Tacere = se taire.
Like tempered steel or a « climat tempéré »: optimism tempered by realism.

m: Easy to control or deal with.
e: Latin tractabilis, from tractare (to handle), frequentative of trahere (to pull).
t: Easy to pull, like a tractor pulling a docile cart. Opposite: intractable.
Rubbed so much it’s worn out. A trite cliché.
Same as « vaciller »: a candle flame swaying back and forth.
Win + some: a smile that wins you over. Old English wynn = joy.
